title: Bayesian Inference with Structured Signal: Static Replica Symmetry Breaking on the Nishimori Line in the Planted Spin Glass
abstract: A common assumption in theoretical models of Bayesian inference is that the signal has i.i.d. components. To study the effect of correlations in the signal prior, we consider a minimal model: the planted spin glass on random regular graphs, where the signal is sampled from an Ising model with coupling $κ$. Depending on the phase of the prior, we find that adding structure in the signal can either help or hinder inference. In the paramagnetic regime, correlations in the signal lower the reconstruction threshold, so that weaker signal strength is sufficient for recovery. In the ferromagnetic regime, the prior alone already enables partial recovery, and we identify the threshold above which the observations provide additional information. When the prior itself is in a replica symmetry breaking (RSB) phase, we detect a static RSB transition in the posterior under Nishimori conditions. This provides an example where a non-separable, correlated prior leads to static RSB in a Bayes-optimal inference problem. We discuss the consequences of this glassy phase for algorithmic performance, in particular for Belief Propagation.
summary: This paper analyzes Bayesian inference in a structured spin glass model, moving beyond simple independent assumptions. By using advanced techniques like the replica method on random regular graphs, it demonstrates that correlated priors can lead to static Replica Symmetry Breaking (RSB) in the posterior distribution. This highlights how structural correlations fundamentally alter the information recovery process in disordered systems.
main_problem: The study investigates how structural correlations within the signal prior affect the feasibility and performance of Bayesian inference in a planted spin glass model, moving beyond standard i.i.d. assumptions.
main_result: The analysis reveals that structured priors can induce static Replica Symmetry Breaking (RSB) in the posterior distribution under Nishimori conditions, providing a non-trivial example of glassy behavior in an optimal inference setting.
method: The work employs advanced tools from statistical physics, including the replica method and cavity equations, to analyze the phase diagram and transition points.
model_or_system: The model is a planted spin glass on random regular graphs. The signal prior is defined by an Ising Hamiltonian with coupling $\kappa$, and observations are noisy couplings $J_{ij}$ related to the true signal $\mathbf{s}$.
key_observables: Reconstruction threshold ($ eta_c$), overlap ($O(\mathbf{s}, \hat{\sigma})$), complexity ($\Sigma_0(x_0)$), and the identification of static RSB transitions.
important_parameters: Signal structure parameter $\kappa$, observation strength $ eta$, and graph connectivity (e.g., 3-regular graphs).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the replica method, cavity equations, and approximations like assuming delta distributions for message passing in the thermodynamic limit.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase diagrams showing regions of paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, and static RSB behavior based on $\kappa$ and signal strength. Other figures plot complexity measures ($\Sigma_0$) to locate transition points.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the Bayesian inference problem by deriving cavity equations for both the prior and posterior distributions. It then uses RSB analysis (replica method) to map out the phase diagram, identifying critical thresholds where the system transitions between different glassy phases.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the methodology of analyzing complex energy landscapes and phase transitions via replica methods is foundational for understanding quantum many-body systems, especially those exhibiting glassy dynamics or frustration.
